doc.title: Language Features
doc.paragraph:
In this section, you will be guided through the features of Adaptive Script. If you know ECMAScript (JavaScript),
lists where the two are the same and where they differ.

A variable gives a name to a value so you can use it again later. You declare one with let, when you plan to assign it again, or with const, when you do not. A variable can be used from its declaration to the end of the block it is declared in.
Adaptive Script does not have classes. Every value has an Adaptive data type, and what you can do with a value is provided by functions that work on that data type.

At this time, Adaptive Script does not support importing code from other locations. To share code between scripts, store it in qualified variables that the scripts can reach, such as an application's qualifiedVariables.

Every value has an Adaptive data type, and a value is never quietly converted from one data type to another: when you want a date from a string, you say so with a typed literal such as "2026-10-11"date, or with to_date(s). Data Types and Conversion shows how.

You can also annotate variables, parameters, and returns with types (integer, string, arrays, object shapes, unions, and more). A data type you write is checked whenever the script runs, and turning type checking on adds checks at compile time and for object shapes. See the Types section for syntax and flags.

Adaptive Script supports closures. A function made inside another function can use the variables and parameters around it, and it keeps them after the outer function has returned, so each later call still sees them. This works for a nested function declaration and for a function value that another function returns. In the example below, each call to make creates a function that remembers its own v:
Every statement ends with a semicolon.
An expression on its own is not a statement: a call, an assignment, ++, and -- are.
Adaptive Script provides try/throw/catch/finally exception handling.

In Adaptive Script, throw is a statement that requires a string (the error message). Write optional data and then any value to store on the error object. Write optional id and then a string that sets the error object's id (for example not_found) so an uncaught error can use that name's HTTP status. After the message, data is only the clause name, so a variable also named data is throw "…" data data.

The catch statement always receives one error object, which contains the message and data that was thrown. The catch binding may be a simple name or a list/object Pattern (same destructuring as let / const), for example catch ({ message, data }). The object also has an id (mnemonic such as throw, not_found, or denied) and a numeric errorCode. Branch on id. If the error is not caught, an HTTP request uses that code's mapped status (for example not_found is 404). general is the default code when nothing more specific applies.
These are the ids you will meet most often in a catch:

row.column: a throw statement without an id
a value of the wrong data type, or out of range, was given to a function or operator
text could not be read as the data type asked for, as in to_integer("1.5")
a value that is needed was undefined
a frozen value, or a const, was changed
source text did not compile, as with eval of a bad script
an object does not exist, or access to it is not permitted

doc.paragraph: The Throw statement in Statements lists the ids a script may throw itself.

A parameter of a function may be a simple name, or the same kind of destructuring pattern you can use with let and const, so a function can take an options object and pick out the properties it needs, with defaults for the ones that are missing. A default may be any expression. A function can also collect the rest of its arguments with ...rest, and a call can spread an array into separate arguments with f(...array). The Function statement in Statements has examples.

A script function declared : void is a procedure: you call it for what it does, not for a value, just as you call the built-in print(). Its call is the void value, not undefined and not the last value assigned in the body, so calling it as a statement does not change the script result. A function with no return type that finishes without returning a value gives undefined, and that call does set the script result.

What you do with objects and arrays is provided by Adaptive functions in the environment. Any of them can be called in method form, with the value first: obj->keys() is keys(obj), and arr->push(1) is push(arr, 1).

There are functions to list an object's properties (keys, values, entries), to read an entry (at), to use an array as a stack or a queue (push, pop, shift, unshift, splice), to make an array of a given length (create_array), to make a value immutable (freeze), and to ask whether every or some entry passes a test (every and some, or all_of and any_of). You can also leave out a value between commas in an array literal, and that entry is undefined. Objects and Arrays covers all of this, and the Function Reference has each function under the categories object, array, and higher_order_array.

A property name in an object may be an identifier, a string literal, or an expression in square brackets. An expression in brackets is evaluated when the object is, and its result, a string, becomes the property name, just as obj[expression] reads or assigns a property. The names of variables and parameters are always identifiers.

At this time, Adaptive Script does not support generators or user-defined iterators. You walk an array, or the characters of a string, with for-of. To walk an object, walk its keys, values, or entries, for example for (let pair of entries(o)).
At this time, Adaptive Script does not support asynchronous operations.

Sometimes a script has the source of another script as a value, such as one stored in an object. To run it, hold it in a script value and pass that to eval, which compiles it and evaluates the result. The same works for a template. When you will run the same source many times, compile it once with compile and run the compiled value with evaluate each time.
doc.code:
eval(script("1 + 1")); // 2 eval(template("Total: ${1 + 1}")); // "Total: 2"
const unit = compile(script("2 * 3")); evaluate(unit); // 6
doc.paragraph: Code run this way may not access or change any variables of the script that runs it. evaluate on its own does not compile anything: evaluate("1 + 1") is just the string "1 + 1".
The switch statement normally compares its value with each case for equality, but with using you can give it a function to compare them any way you like, such as matching a regular expression.
A script may include a #compile pragma to control how the compiler treats it, such as whether type checking runs. The Types section lists the environment flags and the matching #compile options.

#compile strictDouble; (flag compile:strictDouble) makes IEEE 754's invalid operation and division by zero exceptions errors for that script. Without it, doubles follow IEEE 754's default handling: 0.0 / 0.0 is NaN and 1.0 / 0.0 is Infinity. With it, those are errors, as are Infinity - Infinity, sqrt(-1.0) and log(0.0), and <, <=, >, >= are IEEE 754's signaling comparisons, an error for a NaN. What IEEE 754 does not call one of those exceptions is unchanged: overflow gives an infinity, a NaN operand passes through arithmetic, and == is the quiet compare. The pragma applies to the script it is in, wherever its functions are called from.

A compiler literal is a # name for a value the compiler already knows. It is a value in an expression, not a statement and not a function call. These are not the same as the #compile pragma or the #block forms used when decompiling.

list.item: #pi, #e, #ln2, #ln10, #log2e, #log10e, #sqrt2, #sqrt1_2: π, e, ln 2, ln 10, log2 e, log10 e, √2, and √½, for the math functions (cos(#pi), log(#e)).
#doubleMax, #doubleMin, #doubleMinSubnormal, #doubleEpsilon: IEEE double limits. #doubleMin is the smallest normal double (C's DBL_MIN) and #doubleMinSubnormal the smallest subnormal one.

#integerMax, #integerMin: the 64-bit integer limits. #integerMaxExactDouble, #integerMinExactDouble: the range (9,007,199,254,740,991 either way, 2^53 - 1) where every integer converts to a double and back unchanged, and survives a JavaScript client reading the JSON.
#infinity (alias #inf), #minusInfinity, #nan: the same as Infinity, -Infinity and NaN. The # forms are preferred, and decompile writes them; the reserved words keep working.
